% Reproduced photographic and screenshot plates.
% Generated by hand from tex/figs/SELECTED.md; see tex/PERMISSIONS.md before posting.
%
% One command per figure. A section author places a plate by writing, e.g.,
%   \plateLeapOverview
% at the point in the section where the float should be anchored, once: a plate
% called twice prints twice, on two pages, under two numbers. Single-column
% plates use `figure`; anything whose labels stop being legible below about
% 8.8 cm uses `figure*` and floats to the top of a page. `[tb]` was tried on the
% single-column plates and moved nothing: where a plate lands pages after its
% anchor, a full-width table is holding the page tops in between, not the spec.
%
% Every plate credits its source inside its own caption, with \src. Seven carry
% \licensed as well, because their source is CC BY 4.0 and the licence asks for
% an attribution line: one line under the caption, naming the work, the licence
% and the change made to the plate. No plate prints a permission status. That is
% a working note, it is held in tex/PERMISSIONS.md, and Appendix A states where
% each plate stands; when a permission comes back, the register is what changes.

% =============================================================== Sec. III, hands

\newcommand{\plateLeapOverview}{%
  \begin{figure*}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.66\textwidth]{figs/selected/hand_leap_overview.png}
    \caption{A low-cost hand in which each actuator \emph{is} a joint: the motor
      bodies are the phalanges, and the bracket-and-spacer stack sets the
      kinematics. The same hand in power and precision grasps on everyday
      objects.\src{\cite{leap_hand_2023}}}
    \label{fig:hand-leap-overview}
  \end{figure*}}

\newcommand{\plateHandScale}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/selected/hand_scale_to_human.png}
    \caption{Five research hands photographed to scale beside an adult human hand
      and a ruler. A count of actuated degrees of freedom says nothing about the
      size of the hand that carries them.\src{\cite{leap_hand_2023}}}
    \label{fig:hand-scale}
  \end{figure}}

\newcommand{\plateIldaLinkage}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.60\columnwidth]{figs/selected/hand_ilda_linkage.png}
    \caption{A fully actuated linkage hand with the transmission left exposed:
      every joint is driven through its own metal four-bar and lead screw, with a
      coin for scale. Greyscale; the source
      photograph is near-monochrome~\cite{ilda_hand_2021}.}
    \label{fig:hand-ilda}
    \licensed[panels (a) and (b), greyscale]{Fig.~5 of Kim et al.,
      \emph{Nat. Commun.} 12:7177}{CC BY 4.0}{https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/}
  \end{figure}}

\newcommand{\plateCoupledLinkage}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.78\columnwidth]{figs/selected/hand_coupled_linkage.png}
    \caption{Where the actuator count is cut: an anti-parallelogram linkage ties
      the distal joint to the proximal one, so one motor sweeps two joints and the
      finger's reachable set is a curve rather than a surface.\src{\cite{bidexhand_2025}}}
    \label{fig:hand-coupled-linkage}
  \end{figure}}

\newcommand{\plateInspireTactilePad}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/selected/hand_inspire_tactile_pad.png}
    \caption{Compliance added after the fact: a printed pad over a foam layer,
      fitted to a commercial hand to spread contact that the rigid shell
      concentrates. The right panel shows the whole hand once
      padded~\cite{articulated_tools_inhand_2025}.}
    \label{fig:hand-inspire-pad}
    \licensed[cropped to the right half]{Fig.~4 of Atar et al., arXiv:2509.23075}{CC BY 4.0}{https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/}

\newcommand{\plateDigitFingertips}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/selected/hand_digit_fingertips.png}
    \caption{Vision-based tactile sensors used as the fingertips themselves: each
      unit is a camera and an illuminated gel, and the sensor body sets the
      fingertip's size and shape.\src{\cite{digit_2020}}}
    \label{fig:hand-digit}
  \end{figure}}

% ========================================================== Sec. IV, simulators

\newcommand{\plateIsaacGymEnvs}{%
  \begin{figure*}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figs/selected/sim_isaacgym_inhand_envs.png}
    \caption{Three in-hand environments as the GPU simulator actually presents
      them. The copies receding into the background are the other parallel
      environments sharing the step; the foreground scene is one of
      thousands~\cite{isaacgym_2021}. The plate shows NVIDIA product imagery;
      CC BY 4.0 conveys no trademark rights.}
    \label{fig:sim-isaacgym-envs}
    \licensed[re-rendered]{Fig.~13 of Makoviychuk et al., arXiv:2108.10470}{CC BY 4.0}{https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/}
  \end{figure*}}

\newcommand{\plateTendonModel}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/selected/sim_tendon_model.png}
    \caption{A tendon-driven hand as the physics engine sees it: spatial tendons
      (green) routed over wrapping cylinders (yellow) inside the transparent
      shell. The routing geometry, not the joint limits, is what a sim-to-real
      gap on this hand is made of.\src{\cite{openai_rubiks_cube_2019}}}
    \label{fig:sim-tendon}
  \end{figure}}

\newcommand{\plateConvexDecomposition}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/selected/sim_convex_decomposition.png}
    \caption{The object the policy touches is not the object it sees. Left, the
      visual mesh; centre, its single convex hull; right, the convex decomposition
      that restores the concavities contact needs.\src{\cite{dexremoe_2025}}}
    \label{fig:sim-convex}
  \end{figure}}

\newcommand{\plateTactileInterpenetration}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/selected/sim_tactile_interpenetration.png}
    \caption{Interpenetration rendered as a field. A compliant contact model
      turns the depth by which object and sensor overlap into the tactile image
      and the distributed force the policy reads; the overlap is the signal, not
      an artefact to be removed~\cite{isaaclab_2025}. The plate shows NVIDIA
      product imagery; CC BY 4.0 conveys no trademark rights.}
    \label{fig:sim-tactile-penetration}
    \licensed[cropped to four panels]{Fig.~10 of Mittal et al.,
      arXiv:2511.04831}{CC BY 4.0}{https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/}
  \end{figure}}

\newcommand{\plateDexpilotStudio}{%

\newcommand{\plateBidexExoskeleton}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/selected/teleop_bidex_exoskeleton.png}
    \caption{The other end of the same problem: a worn bimanual exoskeleton that

\newcommand{\plateRetargetEmbodiments}{%
  \begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/selected/teleop_retarget_embodiments.png}
    \caption{One human hand pose, four robot hands. The same tracked keypoints
      retarget to visibly different postures on each mechanism, which is the size
      of the embodiment gap a shared demonstration corpus has to
      cross~\cite{anyteleop_2023}.}
    \label{fig:teleop-retarget-embodiments}
    \licensed[panels re-laid out as a column]{Fig.~10 of Qin et al., arXiv:2307.04577}{CC BY 4.0}{https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/}
  \end{figure}}

\newcommand{\plateRetargetArtifacts}{%
  \begin{figure*}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figs/selected/teleop_retarget_artifacts.png}
    \caption{What retargeting gets wrong, magnified. Against the same source
      motion, two established methods place the fingertip off the object, drive it
      through the surface, or hyperextend a joint; the failure is in the contact
      set, not in the joint-angle error a retargeting method usually reports.\src{\cite{toporetarget_2026}}}
    \label{fig:teleop-retarget-artifacts}
  \end{figure*}}

\newcommand{\plateArcticDataset}{%
  \begin{figure*}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figs/selected/data_arctic_bimanual.png}
    \caption{A bimanual hand-object capture, from source video to the fitted
      meshes and the dense contact field between them. The contact annotation is
      inferred from tracked geometry, which is why its accuracy is bounded by the
      fit rather than measured at the surface.\src{\cite{arctic_2022}}}
    \label{fig:data-arctic}
  \end{figure*}}

% ========================================================== Sec. VI, two hands

\newcommand{\plateHandoverAllegro}{%
  \begin{figure*}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figs/selected/bimanual_handover_allegro.png}
    \caption{Two arms and two four-fingered hands as thrower and catcher, with the
      observation and action dimensions each policy sees. The hands never touch:
      the coupling between them is the object's flight.\src{\cite{dynamic_handover_2023}}}
    \label{fig:bimanual-handover}
  \end{figure*}}

\newcommand{\plateGraspPenetration}{%
  \begin{figure*}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figs/selected/bimanual_grasp_penetration.png}
    \caption{The failure modes of synthesised two-hand grasps, with the contact
      region enlarged: fingers inside the object, fingers inside the other hand.
      At the scale of the whole grasp all four look plausible, which is why a
      success rate quoted without a penetration measure says
      little~\cite{bimangrasp_2024}.}
    \label{fig:bimanual-penetration}
    \licensed[cropped to Fig.~9 alone]{Fig.~9 of Shao and Xiao, arXiv:2411.15903}{CC BY 4.0}{https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/}
  \end{figure*}}
